rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi thinks the Jews probably raised the question through Quraysh to unsettle the Prophet and hinder the true call, as with the sleepers of the cave.
rows.anchor: to make the Prophet (sws) anxious and worrisome and to implant hurdles in the path of the true call.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Jews were deeply interested in Dhū al-Qarnayn, whom they regarded as a benefactor king and whose name appeared in their prophets’ scriptures.
rows.anchor: their benefactor king, as will be seen from later details. He is also mentioned in the scriptures of their prophets.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an answers because Dhū al-Qarnayn’s life could instruct the arrogant people enslaved to worldly desires discussed throughout the sūrah.
rows.anchor: the life of Dhū al-Qarnayn could have offered a lesson of life to these arrogant slaves of worldly desires

rows.speaker: Exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes generally identify Dhū al-Qarnayn as Alexander; some identify him as Cyrus or Darius, and another opinion names a Himyarite king.
rows.anchor: Generally, he has been regarded to be Alexander. Some regard him to be Cyrus or Darius, who were Persian kings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Himyarite identification has no argument worthy of mention.
rows.anchor: There is no argument worthy of mention in favour of this opinion.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alexander does not fit the Qur’anic portrait of a monotheist, afterlife believer, just ruler, or conqueror of the stated reach, and there is no evidence for the title.
rows.anchor: None of these qualities existed in Alexander.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Darius made eastern and western conquests but was not a pioneer; he consolidated the empire Cyrus had established.
rows.anchor: his status is not that of a pioneer. He only consolidated the empire established by Cyrus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus is a plausible identification because he was faithful and just, and the Qur’an’s three campaigns include two verified by history and signs supporting a third.
rows.anchor: He was a man of faith and a very just ruler whose magnanimity has been praised by both old and new historians.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus freed the Jews from Babylonian slavery, helped rebuild the Temple, and had been foretold by Jewish prophets.
rows.anchor: he had liberated them from their slavery in Babylon and by his help the Temple was once again built.

rows.speaker: Daniel
rows.claim: Daniel’s vision describes a two-horned ram, with one horn longer and growing later, that charges west, north, and south without resistance.
rows.anchor: I looked up, and there before me was a ram with two horns, standing beside the canal, and the horns were long.

rows.speaker: Gabriel
rows.claim: Gabriel interprets the horns as Media and Persia, the kingdoms the promised king would conquer; Cyrus conquered both and thus is called Dhū al-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: Gabriel explained this vision to Daniel by saying that the two horns refer to the two kingdoms of Media and Persia

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A statue of Cyrus was found at Estakhr, built under Ardashir I, with two horns visible on its crown.
rows.anchor: One of his statues has been discovered in recent times in Estakhr, an ancient city of Persia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statue’s horns may symbolize Cyrus’s majesty and power or his conquests of Media and Persia.
rows.anchor: they are etched to portray his majesty and power or it may be because of these two conquests referred to above.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi suggests that the Jews of Arabia gave Cyrus the title Dhū al-Qarnayn.
rows.anchor: given to Cyrus by the Jews of Arabia.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is an appeal: if asked, the Prophet will narrate part of the story in the hope that listeners attend and benefit.
rows.anchor: hopefully you will listen to it intently and benefit from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word dhikr carries the sense of reminding and learning a lesson.
rows.anchor: The meaning of reminding and learning a lesson found in the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse’s sabab refers to the means and resources with which Cyrus’s kingdom was provided.
rows.anchor: blessed him with means and resources of all kinds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus became governor of his father Cambyses’ small kingdom of Anshan in the mid-sixth century BCE and then fought Media’s ruler.
rows.anchor: he was appointed the governor of a small kingdom called Anshan of his father Cambyses.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus won a major victory and soon conquered the great kingdoms of his age, ruling from Balkh and Makran to the Roman Sea.
rows.anchor: earned a huge victory. In the remaining few years, he conquered all great kingdoms of those times

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb atbaʿa means to pursue something.
rows.anchor: to get after and pursue something.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means evaluating and arranging resources, and by extension preparing for a campaign or expedition.
rows.anchor: From here it came to be used to imply the wider meaning of preparing for a campaign or an expedition.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The western sunset scene means Cyrus reached the sea, the limit of the then-known inhabited world under his sway.
rows.anchor: Now only the ocean lied ahead. It was as if this was the furthermost part of the land inhabited in the west

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus’s first expedition went west from Ecbatana, conquering Media and Lydia, defeating Croesus at Sardis, and reaching the Roman Sea.
rows.anchor: he conquered Media (present day Iraq and Syria) and Lydia (present day Turkey).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The campaign placed new subjects under Cyrus’s authority, leaving him discretion to punish or treat them kindly.
rows.anchor: as a result of this campaign, the subjects he gained were made to submit to his authority

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says Cyrus’s only rightful course was justice and kindness, even though he had the freedom to act unjustly and would be punished for it.
rows.anchor: It was his discretion. The only right he had was to be just and kind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A ruler who acts justly is rewarded by God, while an unjust ruler is punished; David’s instruction supplies the proper standard.
rows.anchor: If he administers justice, he will be rewarded from God and if he is unjust, he will be punished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: David is instructed to govern justly and not follow desire, lest it divert him from God’s path.
rows.anchor: So, deal with justice among people and you must not yield to your desire

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to Dhū al-Qarnayn resembles God’s address to Solomon, which allows him to be generous or withhold generosity.
rows.anchor: is the same as one with Solomon (sws) in the following verse

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison describes people’s freedom to believe or disbelieve and to be generous or stingy after receiving God’s favors.
rows.anchor: freedom to be kind and generous after receiving God’s favours or become stingy.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though people may choose either attitude, only the behavior God demands is pleasing to Him.
rows.anchor: However, in the eyes of God, only one of them is pleasing and it is that what He has demanded from people.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses portray Cyrus’s practice: he punishes oppressors, who also face God’s punishment, and treats believers with kindness while they receive a good fate hereafter.
rows.anchor: Just as the previous statement is the portrayal of a situation, the statement of this verse expresses practice.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source cites the Jews’ words in 2:93 as an example of Qur’anic language portraying conduct or attitude.
rows.anchor: To portray an attitude or practice through the word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about treating the righteous gently also portrays Cyrus’s attitude.
rows.anchor: also similarly portray attitude. Some people merely because

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The use of “We said” and “he said” is not enough to establish that Dhū al-Qarnayn was a prophet; Islahi regards him as a just and compassionate ruler.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, this is not reason enough to regard him to be a prophet.

rows.speaker: Historians
rows.claim: Historians say Cyrus’s army spared conquered cities; he treated subjects kindly, removed taxes, forgave enemies, and preserved Media’s ruler’s royal standing with troops and riders.
rows.anchor: Historians write that the army of Cyrus never harmed the inhabitants of any of the cities it conquered.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage presents Dhū al-Qarnayn as a true monotheist who believed in the hereafter, and history corroborates this.
rows.anchor: Also evident from these verses is that Dhū al-Qarnayn was a real monotheist who had conviction in the hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus followed Zoroaster; original Zoroastrian teachings affirmed God and the hereafter, though later adherents distorted the religion with Dualism.
rows.anchor: Cyrus was a contemporary of Zoroaster and also his follower.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dara’s tablets credit Ahura Mazda with his kingdom and ask for help to govern rightly; Islahi infers Cyrus passed on his religiosity and respected Israelite prophets.
rows.anchor: In his tablets, Dara expresses gratitude to Ahura Mazda (God) and attributes his kingdom to His graciousness.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Cyrus’s second expedition went east to quell rebellious tribes from Makran, Qandahar, and Balkh that troubled Persia’s border; Islahi describes them as uncultured and unfamiliar with house-building.
rows.anchor: the reason for this expedition was the rebelliousness of the tribes of Makran, Qandahar and Balkh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi says this verse shares the context of 21:51: God gave Abraham guidance and authority because He knew his abilities; likewise God knew Dhū al-Qarnayn’s capacity to rule the kingdom He enabled him to win.
rows.anchor: This verse has exactly the same occasion and context as verse 51 of Sūrah al-Anbiyā’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Historians do not record Cyrus’s third expedition, but mention his northeast journey after Babylon; Islahi speculates he headed toward eastern Turkey, died in a pit, and that the dam episode occurred on this journey.
rows.anchor: This is a mention of the third expedition of Cyrus. Historians have not mentioned it anywhere.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Gog and Magog are identified as descendants of Noah’s son Japheth who inhabited northern Asia.
rows.anchor: They refer to the progeny of Japeth son of Noah (sws) which inhabited the northern areas of Asia.

rows.speaker: Hezkiel
rows.claim: Hezkiel’s prophecies place Gog in Magog and describe him coming from the far north.
rows.anchor: The word of the LORD came to me: Son of man, set your face against Gog, of the land of Magog

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi maps Rosh, Meshek, and Tubal to Russia, Moscow, and Tubalsac, placing these regions south of Palestine.
rows.anchor: Rosh, Meshek and Tubal today exist as Russia, Moscow and Tubalsac

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tribes lived south of the Caspian in Central Asia and attacked Persia through Turkey and the Caucasus; Islahi suggests Cyrus filled the pass to stop them.
rows.anchor: They attacked Persia from both Turkey and from the Caucasian pass.

rows.speaker: Travellers and tourists
rows.claim: An iron wall still stands at the Daryal pass in Caucasia and is mentioned in travelogues; the Abbasid caliph Wathiq reportedly sent fifty thousand people to find it.
rows.anchor: Travellers and tourists have also mentioned it in their travelogues.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some attribute the wall to Dara or Nausherwan, but Islahi considers Cyrus the stronger candidate, citing the empire’s southern boundary and the names Koresh and Gora.
rows.anchor: People ascribe this wall to Dara or to Nausherwan. However, stronger evidence indicates that it was constructed by Cyrus.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wall was made of metal between two mountains and left an opening below to drain rainwater.
rows.anchor: This wall has been made by a metal between two mountains. Space has been left in its lower part for rain water to escape.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people could not understand others because isolation left them without contact with other nations or their tongues.
rows.anchor: These people had no interaction with other nations. They had isolated themselves in this land.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quwwa means manpower; Dhū al-Qarnayn declines the offered resources and asks people to help with their labor.
rows.anchor: did not accept the offer of resources made by his subjects; he however asked them to provide manpower.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement about what his Lord provided means Cyrus had enough wealth and had acquired it cleanly, without loot or plunder.
rows.anchor: it is also clean; it was never earned through loot and plunder.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zubar is the plural of zabra and means iron slabs.
rows.anchor: It means “iron slabs.” The word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sadaf means space or covering; its dual form points to both mountain edges, so the gap between them is filled, as in the paired east and west in al-Raḥmān.
rows.anchor: The purpose is to convey the fact that the space between both mountains was filled.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dakkāʾ originally refers to a camel’s hump and here means to flatten and level down.
rows.anchor: Here it means to flatten and level down.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The iron wall was so robust that Gog and Magog could neither climb it nor breach it.
rows.anchor: Gog and Magog could not even climb it nor create any fissure in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maryam is paired with al-Kahf: their subjects are similar, while their reasoning and narrative styles differ.
rows.anchor: This sūrah is the counterpart of Sūrah al-Kahf as it forms a pair with it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prophets in Adam’s, Noah’s, and Abraham’s lines preached monotheism, prayer, and zakāh, but their followers turned to polytheism, abandoned the rites, and followed innovations and desires.
rows.anchor: all celebrated prophets born in the progeny of Adam (sws), Noah (sws) and Abraham (sws) preached monotheism.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is urged to persevere against their hostility and is given glad tidings of success.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) is urged to show perseverance on their attitude and given glad tidings of success.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The adversaries mistake worldly success for proof of their truth; it is only respite until the truth is conclusively conveyed and they have no excuse when seized.
rows.anchor: they regard their worldly successes in contrast to the believers to be a reason of their own veracity.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus and Mary are prominent because Christians and Jews secretly supported Quraysh; the Qur’an exposes the People of the Book to show they cannot support a truthless cause.
rows.anchor: the Christians too had begun to secretly support the Quraysh.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Zacharias story introduces Mary’s story and counters Christians who treat Jesus’s miraculous birth as proof of his divinity.
rows.anchor: This incident forms a prelude to the anecdote of Mary (sws) mentioned subsequently.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an is the Prophet’s means to warn and give glad tidings; those receptive will believe, refusers will face their fate, and he need not worry about them.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is told that the Qur’ān is the best instrument to warn people and give them glad tidings.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only believers will succeed on the Day of Judgment.
rows.anchor: Only the believers will succeed on the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding analysis makes the sūrah’s structure and coherence evident.
rows.anchor: the structure and coherence of the sūrah becomes very evident.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening symbols are abbreviated letters; Islahi directs readers to his discussion of al-Baqarah’s opening verse.
rows.anchor: These are from among the abbreviated letters. Detailed discussion on this can be found under the first verse of Sūrah al-Baqarah.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dhikr is used in the sense of the imperative “remember”; the stories are narrated so the Prophet and others may learn from them.
rows.anchor: same meaning as the imperative word

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abdahu affectionately refers to Zacharias; being called God’s servant is a great honor.
rows.anchor: affectionately refers to Zacharias (sws). What can be a greater honour for a person than God Himself calling him His servant?

rows.speaker: Ḥāfiẓ
rows.claim: The cited poem expresses willingness to exchange worldly wealth and status for being accepted as the beloved’s servant.
rows.anchor: if you accept me as your slave, I will abandon the wealth and status of this world in exchange of this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zacharias probably made the prayer while in iʿtikāf at the Temple; private prayer is the foremost etiquette and aids acceptance because it is free of pretension.
rows.anchor: supplicating in private is its foremost etitquette and the best recommendation for its acceptance too.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mentioning that even his bones had become hollow intensifies Zacharias’s description of old age and prepares for his request.
rows.anchor: even his bones have become hollow, what to speak of the outer body.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi reads Zacharias’s words as an appeal to divine mercy: he presents his frailty and reminds God that his past prayers were never unanswered.
rows.anchor: he tried to capture the mercy of God through it. Firstly, he presented his frailty and weakness as a recommendation to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawālī means paternal relatives, brothers, and in-laws; Zacharias feared his poor relatives would fail to continue Jacob’s family traditions and mission, so he sought a successor despite old age and his wife’s barrenness.
rows.anchor: Zachariahs relatives were not good people. He feared that after his death they would not be able to carry on his traditions and that of Jacob’s family

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because God controls all means and is not dependent on them, Zacharias prayed despite little ordinary hope of an heir.
rows.anchor: all means and resources are in God’s hands. God is not dependent on them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A sincere supplication with the right timing, objective, feelings, and wording is accepted; God can bring mercy despite apparently hopeless circumstances.
rows.anchor: When a supplication is made at the right time, with the correct objective, with sincere emotions and with the right selection of words, it is immediately accepted.
